StringWithMarkup.String: Ingestion of the leaves of Acer rubrum (red maple), especially the wilted one in the fall, can cause severe oxidative damage to equine erythrocytes, leading to potentially fatal methemoglobinemia and hemolytic anemia. Gallic acid and tannins from Acer rubrum leaves have been implicated as the toxic compounds responsible for red maple toxicosis. To investigate further how red maple toxicosis occurs, this study used aqueous solutions of gallic acid, tannic acid, and ground dried Acer rubrum leaves that were incubated with contents of equine ileum, jejunum, cecum, colon, and liver, and then analyzed for the metabolite pyrogallol, a more potent oxidizing agent. They found that gallotannins (a class of molecules belonging to the hydrolysable tannins) and free gallic acid are present in Acer rubrum leaves and can be metabolized by the K. pneumoniae and E. cloacae found in the equine ileum to form pyrogallol.

Matched.Citation: Bischoff K. Pyrogallol Toxicosis in Horses. Veterinary Clinics of North America: Equine Practice. 2024 Apr;40(1):77–82. doi: 10.1016/j.cveq.2023.10.001.

StringWithMarkup.String: Maple and pistachio genera plants have been reported to cause acute hemolysis in horses, possibly due to the metabolism of gallic acid to pyrogallol by enteric bacteria. The diagnosis is often tentative and circumstantial. and the treatment is symptomatic and supportive. This can include detoxification, fluid and electrolyte therapy, supplemental oxygen, and pain control. The prognosis is guarded to poor; however, horses that survive six days postexposure are expected to recover.

StringWithMarkup.String: GA is anticipated to be a successful medication for the long-term prevention of DILI because of its weak toxicity in animal and clinical trials. In in vivo models, GA ameliorated liver toxicity induced by CCl4, antineoplastic drugs, NSAIDs, alcohols, biotoxins, antidepressants, anti-tuberculosis drugs, and other environmental toxins. The main mechanisms for GA's reduction of DILI include modulation of CYP450 enzyme activity, regulation of the MAPKs signaling pathway, free radical scavenging, upregulation of Nrf2, and downregulation of NF-κB and pro-inflammatory cytokines.

Section.Description: Lethal dose values describe the amount of a chemical expected to cause death in test subjects under specified exposure conditions. These values are commonly expressed as dose-based toxicity endpoints such as the median lethal dose (LD50), which represents the estimated dose expected to cause death in 50% of the test subjects. Other endpoints include LD0 (no observed deaths) and LD100 (death in all test subjects).

Effect level values describe the dose or exposure level of a chemical associated with observed biological or toxicological effects in test subjects. These dose-based endpoints include Low Effect Level (LEL), No Effect Level (NEL), Lowest Observed Effect Level (LOEL), No Observed Effect Level (NOEL), Lowest Observed Adverse Effect Level (LOAEL), and No Observed Adverse Effect Level (NOAEL), which represent exposure levels associated with observed or unobserved effects or adverse effects under specified exposure conditions.

StringWithMarkup.String: Gallic acid's production and use in photography, writing ink, dyeing, manufacture of pyrogallol, paper manufacture, pharmaceuticals, engraving of lithography, and as an analytical reagent may result in its release to the environment from its use. If released into the atmosphere, gallic acid will exist both in the vapor phase and particulate phase in the ambient atmosphere, based on an estimated vapor pressure of 1.2X10-7 mm Hg at 25 °C. Vapor phase gallic acid is degraded in the atmosphere by reaction with photochemically-produced hydroxyl radicals with a half-life of about 3.6 hours. An estimated Koc value of 57 suggests that gallic acid will have high mobility in soil. Volatilization from moist soil is not expected based upon an estimated Henry's Law constant of 8.5x10-20 atm-cu m/mole. Volatilization from dry soil surfaces should not be important given the vapor pressure of this compound. Under both aerobic and anaerobic conditions, gallic acid is mineralized to methane and carbon dioxide in the presence of certain Rhodospirillaceae. Using an activated sludge inoculum, 90.5 percent gallic acid was biodegraded as measured by by COD removal. In water, gallic acid is expected to adsorb to sediment or particulate matter based on its Koc value. This compound is not expected to volatilize from water surfaces given its estimated Henry's Law constant. Bioconcentration in aquatic organisms should be low based upon an estimated BCF value of 2. Given the commercial uses of gallic acid, human exposure appears to be likely from occupational situations through dermal, ingestion, and inhalation routes. General population exposure may result from dermal contact with plants containing tannin and ingestion of tea. (SRC)

StringWithMarkup.String: The rate constant for the vapor-phase reaction of gallic acid with photochemically-produced hydroxyl radicals has been estimated as 108X10-12 cu cm/molecule-sec at 25 °C(SRC) using a structure estimation method(1,SRC). This corresponds to an atmospheric half-life of about 3.6 hours at an atmospheric concentration of 5X10+5 hydroxyl radicals per cu cm(1,SRC). Also, reaction with nitrate radicals may be important(2,SRC). Gallic acid is not expected to undergo hydrolysis(SRC) or direct photolysis in the environment due to the lack of functional groups to hydrolyze or absorption of UV light greater than 290 nm, respectively(3).

Section.Description: Sorption to soils and sediments is an important factor on the transport and fate of organic contaminants in the environment.  The soil/water adsorption coefficient, also known as solid-water distribution coefficient (Kd), measures the amount of chemical substance adsorbed onto soil per amount of water.  Since adsorption occurs predominantly by partition into the soil organic matter, it is more useful to normalize the Kd value to the organic carbon content of a soil and express the distribution coefficient in Koc (organic carbon normalized distribution coefficient).  The greater the Kd (or Koc) value, the less likely a chemical will leach or contribute to runoff.  A very high value means it is strongly adsorbed onto soil and organic matter and does not move throughout the soil.

StringWithMarkup.String: The Henry's Law constant for gallic acid is estimated as 8.5X10-20 atm-cu m/mole(SRC) using a fragment constant estimation method(1). This value indicates that gallic acid will be essentially nonvolatile from water surfaces(2,SRC). Gallic acid's Henry's Law constant(1,SRC) indicates that volatilization from moist soil surfaces is not expected(SRC). Gallic acid is not expected to volatilize from dry soil surfaces based on an estimated vapor pressure of 1.2X10-7 mm Hg(SRC), determined from a fragment constant method(3).
